title: The Standing Where Trees Choose Not to Fall

features.name: the scarred elder
features.desc-on-touch: An ancient eucalyptus, its trunk split from shoulder to root by lightning or fire. It still bears new leaves every spring from both sides of the scar.

features.name: the blackened row
features.desc-on-touch: Trees burnt to their cores, standing as charcoal pillars. The archive numbered them and filed their ring-counts. This was the year 2003.

features.name: the choice marker
features.desc-on-touch: A carved stone set where three burn boundaries meet. The trees here refused the fire twice. The carving says only: THEY HELD.

features.name: the ash shelf
features.desc-on-touch: A ledge of preserved ash where the firebreak was cut. It has not moved in eighteen years, sealed by the archive's own measurement stake.

features.name: the living witness
features.desc-on-touch: A young tree grown in the shade of an older scar. It carries the shape of its mentor in its trunk—learning stillness before it learns growth.

inscription: the forest did not burn because we chose it, but because they—each tree in its own way—chose to hold

file.name: Firebreak_Ecology_2003_Onwards.txt
file.note: Records of the standing grove after the second major fire. Photographs, ring-counts, local interviews. A section marked PERSONAL—DO NOT UPLOAD is still unredacted.

reverie.title: REVERIE — the burnt country, red sky
narr: You stand among the scarred trees as the light goes ember-gold.
She is placing her hand on a trunk still warm from yesterday's
fire crews. The smoke has cleared but not far. She says: they
chose. This tree and this one and this one. Not all of them.
She traces the scar. You understand now that choice is an action
taken by root and grain, not just by people. The air tastes old.

exits.label: back down to the firebreak and the wind's choice
deeper into the standing forest that keeps choosing to remain
toward the unburnt country where the same choice is still being made
to the blackened ridges where other fires have written their names
